newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts see Russia accepting limited NATO growth.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Russia accepting limited NATO growth.

text.p: A U.S.-Russia summit next week could show Moscow giving grudging acceptance of NATO membership for former members of the Warsaw Pact, the now-defunct east bloc military alliance, an independent Swedish think-tank said on Monday.

But Moscow would remain implaccably opposed to republics of the former Soviet Union, such as the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, joining the Western Alliance, analysts at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) said.

"They will accept the first wave but not enlargement unlimited in space and time, they will accept expansion to the former Warsaw Pact territories but not the former Soviet Union, the institute's director, Adam Daniel Rotfeld, said.
He was speaking at a news conference unveiling a SIPRI study of Russia's defence relationship with Europe.
Presidents Bill Clinton of the United States and Boris Yeltsin of Russia are scheduled to meet in the Finnish capital, Helsinki, on March 19 and 20 for what Clinton has predicted will be tough talks.

NATO country leaders are expected at a July meeting in Madrid to invite some of Moscow's former allies -- the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are considered front-runners -- to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
Russia has repeatedly condemned such plans as a threat to its security, likely to jeopardise its relations with the West.

Moscow on Monday said that talks between Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solan had been "positive" but alliance diplomatic sources said major differences remain over Russian insistence on a freeze on new military installations by future members.

SIPRI project-leader Vladimi Baranovsky said that Yeltsin might seek guarantees that countries such as the Baltic states and other former Soviet republics would not be future candidates for NATO membership.
Clinton could not agree to such terms, a diplomat said.
Lena Jonson, of the Swedish Institute of International Relations, predicted that the summit could produce agreement on broad issues but leave substantive details unresolved.
"The devil is in the details and there may be lack of agreement in the details," she said.

The SIPRI study, "Russia and Europe: The emerging security agenda", said that Russia was still very much in a state of transition from a totalitarian command economy to a market-driven democracy and its relations with the outside world remained potentially explosive.

It listed as some areas of concern the social side-effects of Russia's battered economy, the risk of ethnic and territorial conflicts within the country, unrestrained rivalry between political groups operating without established rules of behaviour and the political activity of senior military officers.

SIPRI'S Rotfeld warned that if Russia were to feel excluded from international decision-making as a result of its diminished size and power the result could be growing influence for its hard-line nationalists.
"Ostracism and isolation of a great power paves the way for extremists," he said.
